en: Preface to the Direct Explanation of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states: "Because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill; when the illness of all sentient beings is extinguished, then my illness is extinguished.
How profound is the great compassion of the Bodhisattva in his deep pity for sentient beings! How ultimate is its reach! Regarding the *Bhaiṣajyaguru*:
The *Sūtra on the Merit of the Fundamental Vow of the Master* is a divine prescription for shedding the shackles of illness and a secret formula for reviving the life of wisdom.

Formerly, when our Buddha traveled and transformed beings in the city of Vaiśālī, he responded to the request of Mañjuśrī and proclaimed this scripture, adapting it to the capacities of those in the age of the Semblance Dharma.
Since its translation and transmission by the Tripitaka masters, its influence has been vast, providing clothing and shelter for all under heaven through its pervasive conditions.

At a time when the teachings are widely heard and upheld, why is it that many find them obscure? It is likely because the scriptures are so concise and simple that their merit and efficacy seem difficult to fathom.
Recently, there was a śramaṇa named Lingyao from the ancient Qingliang Monastery in Zhejiang, who dwelt within the field of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and roamed the garden of the written word.
Using speech to express the ineffable and providing an interpretation where there is no [fixed] solution, he composed a commentary on this scripture titled *Zhí*.
The brilliance of this commentary’s prose is so radiant that it naturally possesses the spirit to pierce the constellations of the Ox and the Cow.
Consequently, I have repeatedly examined the commentaries of various masters and realized that Master Yao’s exegesis stands apart with its own unique insight and perspective.

Thereupon, disregarding my own lack of self-measure, I have annotated the margins and committed this work to the printing blocks for eternal transmission to the world. Indeed, all sentient beings harbor the three obstructions...
Chronic illness has caused them to undergo the cycle of the six realms for countless kalpas; they remain unaware of how many eons have passed.

Only when the Precious Buddha of the Blue Emperor thoroughly exhausted his compassionate heart did he mount the wheel of the twelve vows to respond to conditions according to their needs, such that there was nothing he did not heal. How magnificent!
The methods of compassion employed by these ancient Buddhas transcend the waters of the Upper Pond by a vast distance. Yet, alas, human hearts are so base and inferior, and furthermore—
Lacking far-reaching vision, their prayers and supplications are moved solely by thoughts of longevity and wealth; they carry hemp while casting away gold—a sight truly worthy of lamentation.
Who would have known that these inverted desires of the three realms could be gradually guided and transformed?
Their ultimate aim and profound purpose all originate from the practice of the very depths. Alas! If one attains the root, the branches will naturally be governed.
If one loses its fundamental essence and merely pursues matters such as longevity and abundance, is this not to be ignorant of the Great Physician’s original vow to deliver sentient beings?
Written on the morning of the full moon in the first month of autumn in the third year of the Jōkyō era (1686).
Preface to the Direct Explanation of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*, compiled by the Bhikṣu Huìjiān of Ān-yǎng Lǜ-śí on the eastern shore of the lake, with palms joined in reverence.

Regarding the sacred teachings that gradually spread to the East, there are frequently many commentaries and sub-commentaries; for instance, those on the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* often number in the hundreds or tens, yet regarding the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*...

Why is it that there is no commentary? The ancients meant that while the Qin burned the scriptures, the scriptures survived; yet when the Han exhausted their efforts in exegesis, the true meaning of the scriptures was lost.
This is merely being entangled by the rambling explanations of narrow-minded scholars. The beginning and end of this scripture consist of nothing more than the three dharmas;

like the sun and moon in the sky, they are visible to all who have eyes—direct, immediate, and manifest, requiring no further interpretation. Since I have already provided an explanation, why would one say it is "straightforward"?

This is what is meant by being "straight" rather than "crooked. To twist and force citations, to laboriously match phrases and gloss words, while the correct meaning becomes obscured—this is not straight.
To ramble on at length to compose a literary work and manipulate the lecturer’s mouth, while the three virtues remain entirely withheld—this is not straight.

Now, following this scripture, I shall directly demonstrate its essence, substance, and function as the three causes for sentient beings, which are themselves the three virtues of the realized person.
May those who compose and revise this work rely upon it for understanding and depend upon it for the arousal of practice, just as the light of the sun illuminates all manner of forms.
I have not dared to provide convoluted notes or prolix exegesis to dilute the sacred scriptures;

my interpretation is itself no interpretation, as I look up to embody the ancients’ intent that there is no need for explanatory commentary. Written on the first day of the first month of the year Jihyou by the Tiantai Bhikṣu.

△ I. General Title:
The Sūtra on the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha.

The title serves as the structural framework for this entire sutra and the ultimate destination of its manifold meanings; it must be contemplated with profound depth, yet it must also be presented with simplicity.
This sutra was bestowed by the Buddha under three names: first, to exclusively eradicate karmic obstacles; second, to belong to the stage of realization; and third, for the purpose of circulation.
None of these can serve as a comprehensive heading that encompasses both the beginning and the end, so it may be left as it is without further discussion. However, [the title] alone...
The title *The Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha* encompasses all meanings and provides a comprehensive framework for the entire sutra;
thus, the correspondence between its general and specific aspects is a source of excellence. By investigating the name, one recognizes the essential intent, and the five meanings become clear.
If one were to present it directly, the title would be based on the person and the dharma, while its essence consists of the profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas, characterized by their vows.
Taking the practice of skillful means as its essence and the merit of uprooting [suffering] as its function, this Mahāyāna teaching is characterized by the "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) stage.
First, regarding the explanation of the title, there are both general and specific aspects. To begin with, the specific names are explained:

"Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha Tathāgata" is the name of the person, and "Merit of Original Vows" is the name of the Dharma; both fully embody the secret treasury of the three dharmas of the Bhaiṣajya.
This is truly because the sentient beings of the nine realms possess the diseases of retribution, karma, and afflictions;

thus, out of the Tathāgata’s great compassion of same-nature, he could not help but attain supramundane utility, using the medicinal herbs of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to universally treat all ailments, which is what is called "medicine.
As for the disease of retribution, sentient beings provisionally take the four great elements to constitute their bodies.
Thus, when one of the four great elements is out of harmony, one hundred and one diseases arise; when all four great elements are out of harmony, four hundred and four diseases suddenly emerge.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* further discusses how the external influences of the four seasons—when cold and heat do not accord with one another—make the body the root of suffering.
When suffering oppresses the body, it expands into immeasurable afflictions and physical maladies, such that there is nothing in the world that does not [afflict] it.
Since there are no sentient beings who are without transgression, there are likewise no sentient beings in the world who are without illness.

Therefore, one should appropriately employ the medicines of worldly precepts, the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), and so forth, to treat the root of the disease; furthermore, one should employ medicines derived from metals, stones, plants, and trees to treat the superficial symptoms of the disease.
The "disease of karma" refers to the five karmas and ten unwholesome actions—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and so on—that sentient beings have accumulated.
These equal offenses constitute active evil causes arising from the body and speech; through the seven limbs of mindfulness, one constructs boundless great sins.
One should employ the medicines of the desire realm, the preparatory stages (*anāgamya*), the four dhyānas, and the eight liberations to pacify the coarse afflictions of the body and speech.

Furthermore, there are three [afflictions]: first, the disease of views and thoughts; second, the disease of the *rajas* and *sāṃsārika* [defilements]; and third, the disease of ignorance (*avidyā*). One should...

Within the twenty-five kingly samādhis, one uses the medicine of emptiness to treat the diseases of views and afflictions, the medicine of the provisional to treat the disease of the dust-like and sand-like [delusions], and the medicine of the middle to treat the disease of ignorance.

Although these medicines can cure diseases, if they are not administered by a skilled person, the medicine will instead become harmful; even the finest *amṛta* (clarified butter) becomes a poisonous drug.
It is like the old physician who used milk as medicine; his demonic and heterodox treatment was not only useless but actually harmful.
Now, those who prescribe medicine and call themselves masters are precisely valued for their ability to apply the medicine. One who can practice but cannot explain is a minister of state;
one who can explain but cannot practice is a teacher of the state; one who can both explain and practice is a treasure of the state.

The Tathāgata excels both in practice and in teaching; though he is a Great Physician, he does not treat minor ailments, for even when lesser physicians fold their hands in impotence, a single dose of his Dharma-medicine causes chronic illnesses to be suddenly cured. He is truly a teacher of humanity and a national treasure.

Thus it is said that the Medicine Master is called the "New Physician" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the "Excellent Physician" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; he is also named the "King of Medicine" or the "Great Physician."

The various names such as "King" and so forth are indeed different in name but identical in meaning. However, when the Buddha treats illnesses, his ten bodies manifest accordingly without being restricted to any single aspect;
he is like the physician from Qin and Yue who possessed no fixed medical technique.

If treating a disease of retribution, he manifests as the Elder Flowing Water, Jīvaka, Shennong, the man from Yue, or Cang Gong, employing the methods of inspection, observation, questioning, and palpation with precision.
Excellently renowned for divine skillful arts, he recognizes medicines that are cold, hot, warm, or neutral; he examines diseases of deficiency or repletion, and cold or heat.

Just as when the three factors emerge through conventional designation, the medicine reaches the ailment and the disease is eliminated—those who can, in the snap of a finger, restore the *gao-huang* (the most inaccessible part of the body) and bring life to flesh and bone are truly the physicians of the world. When treating the diseases of karma, he manifests [in various forms].
Entering profound meditative absorption and great samādhi, he acts as a celestial king among the gods of the three realms;

he appears as the Great Brahmā Avalokiteśvara, the Far-Reaching Avalokiteśvara, or as the Tathāgata Tripiṭaka, and so forth. He is thoroughly proficient in the medicinal remedies of the Dharma to counteract various afflictions:
to those with excessive greed, he grants the contemplation of impurity; to those with excessive anger, he grants loving-kindness and compassion; and so on.

To bestow the medicine of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception upon one who has attained concentration in all stages, so that they do not dwell on its flavor or realize it through darkened testimony, is like a horse trainer who both caresses and lashes the horse, taming and protecting it with appropriate skill. This differs from those who practice counting the breath or the impurity of charnel grounds;

it is like applying a bellows to the wrong furnace. Such a person is a physician of inferior response for the sake of meditative concentration; if they were to treat affliction [with such means], it would be a mistake.

The afflictions and illnesses are treated as follows: the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) preaches the medicine of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) to cure the illness of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) preaches the medicine of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) to cure the illness of the "dust-sands" [afflictions];
and the *dharmakāya* (truth body) preaches the medicine of the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) to cure the illness of ignorance (*avidyā*).

This is precisely what is employed in the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, serving as the unsurpassed King of Medicines. As stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), he is the "Excellent Physician."
Only then is he named the Medicine Master, the Perfectly Enlightened One of the East in this Sahā world. Only a Buddha can fully realize and employ [this power];
it cannot be matched by those on lower stages, except for those bound to one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), who are permitted a glimpse of it from below.

Furthermore, one should know that since the merit of the Medicine Master lies in the extraction of suffering, it should be called the function of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). However, as for illness...
Once the distinction has been made, one becomes naturally serene; through successive manifestations, one accomplishes the virtue of liberation.

As for the title "Lapis Lazuli Light" bestowed upon the Medicine Master (Bhaiṣajyaguru), it means that when one gains mastery over the medicinal dharma of the three contemplations, one is able to cure the diseases of the three obstructions and open the great treasury of light of the three wisdoms—this is what is meant by "when defilement is exhausted, clarity arises," and "when purity reaches its limit, radiance penetrates. If...

The World-Medicine cures diseases as retribution; when it possesses radiance, it is like the passage in the sutra where a woodcutter carrying firewood enters the city and a single branch manifests light externally.
Those who recognize it purchase and examine it, finding it to be the body of the King of Medicine Trees (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-vṛkṣa*), which universally cures all ailments.
In this Eastern Land, the personage of Shen Nong has a body like lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out. Whoever consumes even a grain of this worldly gold...
The eighty-four thousand medicinal herbs of the rocks, trees, and grasses all appear within [his vision]:
which enter which meridians, which treat which pathologies, and whether they are toxic or non-toxic. Thus he establishes the true pharmacopoeia as his primary application.

As for the "Ancestor of Medicinal Herbs," Qin Yue-ren, by drinking the water from the upper pond, was able to see through walls and courtyards; when viewing patients with congealed nodules, the people appeared radiant—not only that.
When a person possesses such radiance, it is because the power of medicinal herbs has taken effect.

For instance, if a person regularly consumes restorative medicines such as *bǔtiāndàzào* (Great Creator of Heaven) ginseng and the like, their face will have a white light; or if a blind person encounters the right medicine, they regain their sight.
These are all cases from the mundane world where medical treatments prove effective, curing illnesses and resulting in the manifestation of light. If [it] emerges...
The medicines of the six perfections—worldly morality, concentration, and wisdom—gain their power and generally possess radiance.

Just as when a bhikṣu receives the precepts at the ordination platform and the four *karmavācanās* are completed, the unconditioned light of the precepts of the Buddhas of the ten directions pours down like clouds and canopies into the crown of the practitioner’s head;
this is called "attaining the precepts. One with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is able to see it. If it is the perfect and great precepts (*parivṛta-śīla*), then it is the Brahma... [text ends].
The Net Sūtra states that the name of the precepts is "Light of the Ultimate Meaning. This light is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white;

it is neither form nor mind, nor is it a phenomenon of cause and effect. By donning these robes of the medicinal precepts, one gains power and thus possesses light. It is the same with meditative concentration (*samādhi*):

the twenty-eight heavens are all born from concentration, and each heaven naturally possesses bodily radiance, which is sometimes called "Limited Light" (*parīttābha*) or "Immeasurable Light" (*apramāṇābha*).

The various forms of "light-sound" (ābhāsvara) all belong to the ultimate tranquility where the faculty of light penetrates through the power gained by taking the medicine of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If one cultivates this within the context of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), there is light: for instance, Kāśyapa attained purple light, and the Bhikṣuṇī was born with light due to her generosity;

those who uphold the precepts naturally have the radiant light of morality (*śīla*); when patience reaches its limit, light arises; and from vigor (*vīrya*), light is emitted that illuminates all things.
The Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana burned his own body as an offering to the Buddha, its light illuminating the entire Dharma-realm; this is called true diligence.

His meditative concentration possessed radiance like that of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the eight higher dhyāna stages—all of which have their own luminosity—yet the light of his wisdom was far more abundant.
If one were to align one’s will with that of the present Buddha and share the same direction, it would be like the Vaidūryaprabha of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva emits a blue light that reaches the seat of Śākyamuni; this light is named "Wisdom.

It is like taking the medicine of the Six Perfections to gain strength and manifest radiance. If one takes the superior medicine of the Three Contemplations, one gains strength and manifests radiance;
thus, this light is fundamentally Prajñā, which is most capable of illuminating and breaking through the disease of darkness, possessing great brilliance. However...
Those who attain it differ in depth and magnitude;
when the light of the sun shines, various colors are seen, causing nocturnal creatures to hide and laborers to rise and succeed. Great men receive its radiance, while infants lose their clear vision.
This is the light of the *prajñā*-wisdom of the Bodhisattva. Once the sun has set, the moon is able to illuminate the night.
The clear, cool, and bright illumination is precisely the moon of Nirvāṇa and the Samādhi of Loving-kindness. Now, if the sun and moon emerge, torches have no further use;
yet when encountering the new moon (*sīpāk*), or when the sages and worthies vanish like the moon, one must rely solely upon the light of the stars.

As the ancient saying goes: "Spring stars accompany the thatched hall," meaning the starlight illuminates the night's brightness. If the three luminaries [sun, moon, and stars] were to obscure their radiance...
Thus, by means of a lamp’s light, a thousand-year-old dark chamber can be dispelled by a single lamp;
even if one bores a hole in the wall to share its light, it can still accomplish human affairs—how much more so when the lamps are lit and shine everywhere!

Even if the lamp has not yet been lit and the midnight sky is shrouded in black clouds and mist, a flash of lightning, though brief, can still pierce the darkness. If this is so, how much more so when the light is at its most intense?

Illuminating objects and accomplishing feats, he is like the light of a firefly; as a Bodhisattva in the stage of *upapadya-parinirvāṇa*, he occupies the rank of a secondary sage (*arhat*) and assists with a single mind, thus being like the light of the sun and moon.
As for Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, they previously shared the same karma and the same resolve as Bhaiṣajyaguru and were named Jyotiṣprabha.
Long ago, when the Prince was first born, his bodily radiance did not cease.
The names Dīpaṃkara and Ratnarcis refer to the moment immediately following the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), when one enters the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) in a single kṣaṇa;

because this duration is extremely brief, it is called the "Lightning Flash Samādhi" (vidyutprabhā-samādhi). Upāli, the "Firefly Light" of the Two Vehicles refers to the light of the fireflies of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

because they possess compassion conditioned by dharmas (sadharmālambana-karuṇā) and benefit sentient beings in accordance with the world, the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is all termed "firefly light," as it cannot compare [to the former].

The "Sunlight" is as described above: the light obtained, which may be analyzed into emptiness, or emptiness-and-emptiness, or emptiness-and-provisionality, or the Middle Way—though these divisions differ, they are all equally the light of Prajñā-wisdom.
This wisdom-light analyzes and shatters the darkness and afflictions of the three delusions to reveal the wondrous principle of the Three Truths;
this is what is meant by the statement that unconditioned dharmas possess distinctions. At the ultimate fruit, the Medicine Master is named Lapis Lazuli (Vaidūrya).

As for "Radiance" (Guāng), it is identical to the Western Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Light) in its pervasive clarity throughout day and night, its long-lasting illumination spanning from antiquity to the present, and its brilliant manifestation that ultimately reveals the *prajñā* virtue of the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-āvabhāsa-garbha*). Question:
Since both equally manifest *prajñā*, why is this one not called "Immeasurable Light"? Answer: Because lapis lazuli is fully endowed [with these qualities], it should properly be called *vaiḍūrya*.
“*Li* is translated as 'Azure Lord' (*Qīngdì*). Since Bhaisajyaguru resides in the East and the East belongs to the color blue, his color should appropriately be blue.

Furthermore, as the *Zhèn* direction is the head of all movement, and *jiǎ* (the first day of the sexagenary cycle) represents the image of the wood element’s sprouting and growth, treating illness with medicine values the power to raise the dead and restore life;
it should not be associated with the name of the West, which signifies the withering and killing of metal. This is due to the Dharma..."
The Tathāgata Prajñāguṇa, who was realized through the arousal of the great vow within the title, is the very essence of the Dharmakāya;
he is the fundamental character of the title. This is because the object is suchness and wisdom is suchness, and object and wisdom are merged into one.
When both object and wisdom are forgotten, one responds to conditions and, upon being invoked, manifests as Perfect Enlightenment to extensively treat [the afflictions].

If the *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata is manifested, he employs the medicinal wisdom of analyzing the substance [of phenomena] as empty through the means of precepts, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*) to treat the illnesses of sentient beings’ karmic retribution, views, and afflictions (*kleśa*);
he acts as the physician for the *dharmatā-śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles.

If the *sambhogakāya* Tathāgata is manifested, he employs the medicine of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) which issues forth from the three matters to treat the various [afflictions] of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The Illness [of Suffering] is the Medicine Master of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*); if one realizes the Dharma-body Tathāgata, then one employs the medicine of the wisdom of the threefold contemplation within the single mind to treat the grave illness of ignorance in sentient beings, thereby becoming the Unsurpassed Medicine Master of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*).

It is by means of these three Tathāgatas that one is able to employ the medicinal light of the three wisdoms to treat the illnesses of the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) of sentient beings, thereby attaining the three [bodies].

The title "Medicine Master" (Bhaiṣajyaguru) possesses these three wisdom-medicines, which universally treat the three obstructions within the Dharma-realm, thereby accomplishing the bodies of the three Tathāgatas.
These three dharmas are mutually requisite; none may be lacking. When combined, they are doubly beautiful; when separated, both are impaired.
Furthermore, the three Tathāgatas are the very essence of the Dharmakāya, possessing the three [wisdoms]. The three Prajñās are the Vaidūrya [Wisdom].
The Radiant One (Vairocana) possesses the three [bodies], and the Three Medicine Buddhas likewise possess the three functions of liberation;
each of these three possesses three further aspects, which, when separated, form nine. Within each of these three, there are mutual distinctions of host and guest, primary and secondary.
As clarified in the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal, although there are nine, they are three, and the three are one; thus, their union and separation are sovereign and perfected.
It is the perfection of the three virtues. The merit of the original vow is precisely the person who has realized the fruit of the aforementioned three virtues;
these three dharmas of perfect interfusion are also able to produce the person who realizes the fruit of the three virtues.

This "original" refers to the true essence of the *dharmakāya*, or what is termed the fundamental reality, fundamental nature, fundamental mind, fundamental awakening, the source, the limit of reality, the fundamental substance, and the fundamental ground.

The primordial wisdom, the original vow, the original luminosity, the original ground, the original reality, the original dharma, the originally existing original *tathāgatagarbha*, and the profoundly deep original stage—though these differ, they all point to the ultimate, perfectly complete root of virtue of the Most Holy One.
If one wishes to rely upon this origin to practice and cultivate, there is indeed a sequential order: namely, the original cause, the original fruit, and the original land.

The basis of lifespan, the basis of nirvana, the basis of response and resonance, the basis of supernormal powers, the basis of preaching the Dharma, the basis of retinues, and the basis of benefiting others—the Book says:
"The gentleman applies himself to the root; once the root is established, the Way arises.

Therefore, whether it concerns the cause and effect of one's own practice, or the capacity and object of transforming others, none of these depart from this fundamental basis of the Dharmakāya. The bodhisattvas of the ten directions have thereby reached the ultimate.
This "original name" refers to the Tathāgata, which is precisely the profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas mentioned in the specific passages of the text.

"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) is the essence of the *vijñapti-hetu* (the cause of manifestation). As stated above, although the *dharmakāya*—the true cause—is universally present throughout the ten realms, if it lacks the arousal of the *vijñapti-hetu*, then the primordial *dharmakāya* would suddenly become inferior to that of devas and humans.
Therefore, it is essential to cultivate and perfect the *vipākajñāna* (fruition-wisdom) before it can truly function as such.
How extraordinary! Now, by means of the four great vows and the cultivation of the six perfections, one adorns oneself with merit and wisdom;

thus, original enlightenment (benjue) is manifested, and the light of the *prajñā* that serves as the cause of realization is also called "originally inexhaustible," being named "Lapis Lazuli Light" (*vaidūryaprabha*). As the Sutra says:
"Immeasurable bodhisattva practices, immeasurable bodhisattva vows"—this is it. The two characters "merit" (*guṇa*) and "virtue" (*deya*) constitute the essence (*zong*) of this teaching.

The Tathāgata achieves wondrous function; according to the secular system of posthumous titles, one who has merit is called a "Founder" (Gongzu) and one who possesses virtue is called an "Ancestor" (Zongzu).
Thus, he takes the eradication of evil and the uprooting of suffering as his merit, and the nurturing of life and the cultivation of goodness as his virtue.

During his causal stage, by the power of the King Samādhi, he universally destroyed the evils of the three obstructions and universally generated the goodness of the three virtues. After the merging of object and wisdom, he further relied upon these original merits.
The Medicine of Virtue universally cures the suffering of the three obstacles for all sentient beings and bestows upon them the wondrous bliss of the three virtues.

Generally, in the sutras, matters such as hearing the names of mantras and upholding them are spoken of in terms of "extracting suffering and bestowing bliss," universally causing all to attain the great liberation that is utterly free from burdens. Indeed, when illness departs, one ascends to flight.
The suffering is exhausted and bliss is realized; this is the efficacy of the Dharma-medicine, and thus the Physician King has achieved his merit.
Therefore, he is honored with the title "Medicine Master" (Bhaiṣajyaguru). This means that because he bestowed and extracted [benefits] during the causal stage, he became medicine;

and because he adorned himself through vows and practices during the causal stage, he manifested as Lapis Lazuli Light (Vaiḍūryaprabha); and because he cultivated the nature of non-separation during the causal stage... [the ten thousand virtues].
By practicing the fundamental, one attains the fruit of the Supreme Tathāgata. It is not possible to become a wondrous person of the Three Dharmas without the wondrous Dharma of the Three Virtues;
nor can the wondrous person of the ultimate fruit propagate the harmoniously integrated Three Dharmas.

Although the person and the Dharma differ, their secret treasury is truly identical. Furthermore, it should be understood that it is the person who propagates the Way, not the Way that propagates the person.
My late friend placed his secular name first and his dharma-name last; he asked:

"Since this sutra begins and ends with the single secret treasury of the three dharmas, why is it that the words concerning its essential substance are few, while the words concerning its functional utility are many?

One must understand that the Tathāgata’s cultivation and realization over kalpas involve the internal merging of objective realm and wisdom, much like a person drinking water who knows its coldness or warmth for themselves; there is no need for external testimony.

To explain in detail: even if one were to describe milk to a blind person, what benefit would it bring to one who lacks sight? Therefore, there is no need for excessive discourse; a brief indication is sufficient.
As for the great compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*) as a skillful means following the fruition, its sole purpose is to extract the suffering of birth and bestow the joy of birth;
thus, the wondrous function of its merit ought to be explained in detail. This is especially so regarding the two pillars.

In the interim, he pointed out and extracted the fundamental source, causing [the disciples] to understand that every single thing is nothing other than the total body and great function arising from the established doctrine;
thus, every action is nothing other than the true mark (*dharmatā*), and every matter equally accords with the wondrous source.
Therefore, whether many or few, they are all the three virtues (*triguṇa*); it truly does not depend on the quantity of words and phrases. "Sūtra" is a specific name.

Since these three categories of dharma are identical, the term "sūtra" (經) applies universally; thus, it is self-evident that the *jiaojing* (teaching sūtra), *xingjing* (practice sūtra), and *lijing* (principle sūtra) need not be stated explicitly.
This is fully detailed in the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) and the *Guangzan Jing Shu* (Commentary on the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*). Regarding the provenance of this sūtra:

it was preached by Śākyamuni during the period of the Vaipulya teachings, and it was first [translated] in China during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty by the śramaṇa Huìjiǎn of Lùnyè Monastery.

Translated during the eleventh year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty by Dharmagupta, together with the śramaṇas Faxing and others, at the Translation Hall in the Upper Lin Garden south of the Luo River in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). It was retranslated during the Tang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang, who corrected the text for circulation;
however, it contained only the Exoteric Teachings and lacked the Esoteric Mantras. [This was rectified] during the Tang dynasty by Yijing.
The Tripitaka Master’s translation of the *Saptabuddha-sūtra* contains esoteric mantras.

Later, Yi Jing extracted the essential meanings from the divine mantras and the several phrases preceding and following them—amounting to over four hundred characters, including the words "until awakening" (*yāvat-bodhi*)—and inserted them into Xuanzang’s version.
This further demonstrates that while their applications are distinct, the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are perfectly integrated. [End of] Explanation of Names.

[The preceding section] concludes. Second, taking the profound sphere of action of all Buddhas as its essence—that is, the ultimate, quiescent, and wondrous realm of the person who has realized the fruit—this realm is free from dust and does not belong to cause or effect, yet it serves as the basis for cause and effect, as in the *Avataṃsaka*. Universal... [text continues].

The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states that "Luminous Wisdom" (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*), "Self-Awakened Noble Wisdom" (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), and "Universal Wisdom" (*samanta-jñāna*) are established separately after "Equality" (*samatā*) and "Excellence" (*viśeṣa*).
This reveals that this realm is fundamentally neither cause nor effect, yet it serves as the basis for the causes and effects of equality and excellence.
That which is the Mahāyāna cause is the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); that which is the Mahāyāna fruit is the true nature of all phenomena. This true nature is fundamentally not a cause.
If it is argued that because [the Dharmakāya] is what is attained through causes and conditions, it refers merely to the common, unadorned Dharmakāya shared by those still in delusion—this is not so.
One must understand that the common ultimate reality (dharmatā) has never failed to be the essence;
however, if one now wishes to cause practitioners to initiate cultivation based upon it, they must certainly take the realization of the fruition as their causal mind.
The supreme, quiescent light constitutes the essence of contemplation; it cannot be said to remain within the state of delusion, for its entire substance is what is taken as the model from above.
The Buddhas are the "Tathāgata’s sphere of practice" mentioned in the title, which is the "original character" (benzi) mentioned in the title;
the rest shall await clarification in the commentary.
Third, regarding that which takes the skillful means of vows and practices as its essence, the Sūtra states:

"The immeasurable bodhisattva practices of that Buddha, the immeasurable bodhisattva vows, and the immeasurable skillful means cannot be fully described. These vows consist of both general and specific types. The general are the Three Great Vows; the specific are divided into twelve.
All of these are the *prativedha-hetu* (revealing cause), consisting of the contemplative observation of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). This is what is called "arousing [the mind]."
The *saṃnāha* (armoring) is practiced from the very first thought; thus, the six perfections are fulfilled thereby, the vows are manifested thereby, and the fruit is realized thereby.
This is what is meant by "ultimately employing great compassion to rescue those in distress.

Since such causes and fruits encompass the myriad practices and manifold vows, and because they are cultivated by those of the Perfect and Sudden vehicle, it is said: "The immeasurable bodhisattva practices are inexhaustible."
When the vows and practices of the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable aspirations are exhausted, the wisdom of retribution is manifested, thereby perfecting the wondrous principle of Lapis Lazuli Light.

Furthermore, it is said that "immeasurable skillful means" refers to how, during the causal stage, the Tathāgata employed various subtle and provisional skillful means to sever delusions and realize the truth;
after the fruition was attained, he again utilized various great and powerful skillful means to universally deliver all beings.
It is as stated: "Sentient beings shall all obtain benefits equally through the twelve great vows and by hearing [the Buddha’s] name and making offerings.
Fourth, regarding the function of bestowing and extracting merit: throughout this sutra from beginning to end, it clarifies only the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness.
The twelve great vows are based entirely upon the Four Noble Truths; five vows are based on the Truths of the Path and Cessation, which are for generating wholesome roots and bestowing happiness.

The seven vows for the cessation of suffering and the accumulation of its causes involve the eradication of evil and the uprooting of suffering; within the merit of hearing the Name, they specifically address the extraction of the three poisons.

Regarding the practice of receiving, maintaining, making offerings, and worship, the merit of bestowing and extracting is clarified through both extensive and abbreviated explanations. Within the light of the divine mantra, the acts of bestowing and extracting are presented together.
Although at the end of the sutra there appears to be a partial emphasis on the transformation of karmic obstacles during a degenerate age, [the essence remains complete].
Regarding this compassion that eradicates suffering, its essence consists in the complete fulfillment of the meaning of eradicating suffering and necessarily bestowing happiness;

thus, from beginning to end, it clarifies the functional efficacy of both bestowing [happiness] and eradicating [suffering]. Since each aspect does not depart from the sphere of profound practice, there is nowhere one goes that is not the total embodiment of great function.
Once this function is manifested, it is like the *agada* medicine: wherever it touches, it heals.
Such a person will certainly receive liberation. Regarding the title of the Dharma, it is called "Merit" (*guṇa*); regarding the title of the person, it is called "Bhaiṣajyaguru.

Is this not so? Furthermore, as for the fifth point—that taking the Great Vehicle’s "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) as the characteristic of its teaching—the titles of both the person and the Dharma are identical to those of the Perfect and Wondrous Secret [Teaching].

Regarding the "Treasury" (Zang), its essence, doctrine, practice, and meaning all arise from and culminate in the Perfect [Teaching]. Although the text as a whole may be judged to belong to the three vehicles, it is in fact the sphere of practice of all Buddhas;
who would say it is not identical to the Perfect Vehicle? This concludes the explanation of the general title.
△ Second, the detailed analysis of the text, which has three parts: 1. Introduction; 2. Main Body; 3. Circulation. Now, the Introduction:

Thus have I heard: at one time the Bhagavat was traveling through various countries on his tour of transformation when he arrived at the city of Vaiśālī and stayed beneath the Drumakinnararāja tree, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-six thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Together with kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings— humans and non-humans—
an immeasurable great assembly respectfully surrounded him as he preached the Dharma for them.

These five matters serve as a general proof for all sūtras; by means of traveling and teaching throughout various lands while surrounded by an assembly, they also encompass the *nidāna* (introduction).

The term *bhagavat* contains six meanings—sovereignty (*vaśitva*), brilliance (*tejas*), magnificence (*darśanīyatva*), renown (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*gurutva*)—and among the five types of reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms], it belongs to the category of "not translated due to containing multiple meanings. Nevertheless, it does not appear here under the heading of the Buddha's name.
The term *Bhagavān* has two meanings: first, it reveals the vast abundance of the World-Honored One’s sublime virtues;
second, it signifies that this sutra is complete in both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. Thus, the name contains six meanings and possesses manifold virtues.
The title *Bhagavān* appears in the Esoteric sections; as stated in the *Yogatantra*, it is called *Bhagavatī*, or *Phag-va*, or *Bhag*.

"Gavati" is precisely the meaning of "Bhagavat" (World-Honored One) today; it is merely that the Sanskrit pronunciation differs according to regional dialects, such as the distinctions between the "Chu" and "Xia" styles.
This is truly because this present sutra not only reveals the merits of the original vows but also provides the benefit of secret mantras for destroying evil;
thus, the designation of the "Esoteric Section" (Mibu) is preserved. That he traveled and transformed beings in various countries sufficiently demonstrates the Tathāgata’s compassion.
Having traversed the world and perfected the unsurpassed Way, he forgot his own status as a noble Dharma King of the Golden Wheel;

instead, through great compassion that identifies with all beings, he entered the mud and the water, sorrowfully and earnestly teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever being obstructed by attachment to any single region or corner.
Confucius was one who [concerned himself with] the four quarters of east, west, south, and north.
The likes of Su Qin and Zhang Yi acting as envoys for Yan, Zhao, Qi, and Chu are just like a single cloud over Cangwu that drifts east with the wind one moment and west with the wind the next.
As the *I Ching* says, "not eating at home but benefiting from affairs in the four quarters"—
this refers to the great sages and worthies who, having realized their own perfection, desire to awaken others and thus never fail to set aside their own interests to follow [the needs of others].
People are to be gathered and transformed according to their conditions. As it is said in the Book: "I am one among the people of Heaven who has awakened first;
I ought to awaken these people with this Way. If there were even a single man or woman who did not receive the grace of Yao and Shun, it would be as if I had pushed them myself into a ditch.
Therefore, I cannot bear for even a single day to sit comfortably upon my mat or wear my black robes.
The single character "transformation" (*hua*) refers to: transforming existence back into non-existence; transforming the born into the matured; transforming ordinary beings into sages;

transforming the partial into the perfect; and transforming the provisional into the real. The harmonization of the five periods and the guidance by means of the One Vehicle are all achieved through the Tathāgata’s universal transformation via the four *siddhāntas*.
As for the various kingdoms, they extend throughout the sixteen [great lands], with their fortified cities [standing as witnesses].
Thus, it was beneath the *piyāla* tree that he attained certainty; this is the place where he preached the Dharma and relied upon his kin.

At that time, during his six years of ascetic practice, he relied upon grass and trees to achieve the Unsurpassed Way. When seeking an opportunity to manifest the Dharma, he would gaze at the tree and walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*).

Now, as he wanders to transform beings and rests his feet, he likewise does not leave the tree. This is because dwelling among tombs or beneath trees easily gives rise to the contemplation of impermanence.
Because it is free from the burden of obscuring attachments and cravings, the Buddha’s Vinaya generally prescribes the use of trees in cemeteries as places of residence for the twelve dhūtas;
this is comparable to Confucius’s Apricot Altar (*xìng tán*), each having its own underlying significance.

Although this tree is located in the city of Vaiśālī and is named "Melodious Sound" (*Lèyīn*), the name does not necessarily correspond to reality; rather, the location itself follows the turning of the Dharma.

The environment shifts according to the mind; if an ordinary person were to arrive here, they would perceive only the bitter wind and rain whistling through, longing for their home thousands of li away, such that even pleasant sounds would become objects of suffering.
As it is said, "The sound of the wind and the cry of the crane are both the armies of Jin.
Now, wherever the Dharma King goes, even when combing his hair against the wind or bathing in the rain, these are still perceived as abodes of peace, let alone when he sits beneath lush trees.
The trees, throughout the day, encounter the majestic wind and become subtly cool; one naturally perceives that the wind whistling through the jewel-trees is as abundant as celestial music.
The *bīca* grass possesses five virtues, which may be understood as a metaphor for the pure assembly.
It is only fitting that the *bīca* Bodhisattvas constantly follow [the Buddha], sharing his majestic deportment like wind and tigers, or clouds and dragons. As for...
Do not kings and their subjects, those who possess nations and households, have no urgent affairs of state? Yet they too gather beneath the trees;
you must know that Prince Siddhārtha was a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), to whom the four quarters turned in virtue and from whom the myriad kingdoms came as sovereigns.
Though he possessed the four seas and was noble as a Son of Heaven, he still cast aside his dignity and willingly undertook ascetic practices—how much more so should this be the case for others?
As for those who are inferior, even among the king’s ministers there are none who do not look up to and emulate the Dharma King; they do not crave wealth or honor.
It is said that when the ruler loves to give, his ministers will readily renounce [worldly ties], just as grass bends when the wind blows.

All are able to regard their homes lightly and value the Dharma, following the Buddha as he turns the wheel of the Law. For example, if a king asks, "How can I benefit my country? [the ministers respond accordingly].
The great officers will surely ask, "How can I benefit my house? while the scholars and commoners will surely ask, "How can I benefit myself?
Above and below, they will mutually seek profit and disregard righteousness.

Even the heavenly beings and the eight classes of spirits forget their own manifold blessings, manifold abilities, manifold passions, and manifold skills, serving as the Buddha's defense against insults; it is exactly like this.

When he first attained perfect enlightenment at the Site of Quiescent Extinction (Śāntimārga), the forty-one stages of the Dharma-body Mahāsattvas, along with the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots of virtue had matured over past lives, gathered like clouds enveloping the moon beneath the rustling trees of the wind;
it was truly the Land of Actual Retribution Adorned (Sambhogakāya-vyūha-bhūmi). Given this, is it not fitting that the name of the tree be "Sound of Joy" (Ratana-nirghoṣa)?

For one who expounds the Dharma, this should be an exposition of the causes and conditions for the Original Vows and Merits of the Western [Pure Land], rather than an exposition of the causes and conditions for the Original Vows and Merits of the Eastern [Pure Land].
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (2-1). First, the Question (2-1-1). Furthermore, the question regarding the distinctions among the names of the Buddhas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
bowed toward the Bhagavān with palms joined, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One,
we pray that you will expound upon the names of such Buddhas as these."
"At that time" refers to the conclusion of the exposition of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

"Thus-like" (*rushi*) means "of such a kind," which signifies being identical [to the Buddha of the West], namely, being identical to the name of the Tathāgata in the Western Quarter. △ Second, the inquiry into the merit of the dharma-gate.
Furthermore, by means of the sublime merit of his original great vows, he causes the karmic obstructions of all who hear it to be eliminated;
this is for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings during the period when the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka) prevails.
The merit of these original vows constitutes a distinct gateway for inquiring into the Dharma, which enables all who hear it—beginning with those of inferior capacity—to emerge from their seeking.
The intent behind this discourse lies in the great compassion that seeks to benefit others; this request is not merely for the sake of a fondness for erudition or a delight in abundance.
One must understand that this inquiry immediately addresses the primary theme of the entire sutra.

The first question regarding the Buddha’s name encompasses the title’s "Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Tathāgata," while the second question regarding the Dharma-gate encompasses the title’s "Original Vow."
I pray that the Tathāgata will graciously reveal the remainder of this single great fascicle of scripture. Thus far, we have completed only the two chapters on the merit of the Buddha’s names;

as for the subsequent transformation and the benefit and joy of the Dharma-ending age, these belong to the matters within the merit of the Dharma-gate itself, and there is nothing further to be said apart from this subject.
Only in this way is it revealed that the general and the specific mutually encompass one another, and their meaning is but a single unity.

If one were to depart from the subject at hand and separately establish a discourse on "removing obstacles and benefiting beings," then the general and the specific would become discordant and fail to encompass one another;
this would not only result in inferior phrasing but would also be incorrect in principle. △ Second, the response, which has three parts:
first, expressing approval.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!

Out of great compassion, you have exhorted me to speak the names of the Buddhas and the merits of their original vows, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to those sentient beings who are entangled by karmic obstructions during the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails. Listen attentively now."
I shall explain it for you with thorough reflection.
The two lines beginning with "In order to uproot karmic obstacles" clarify the words of exhortation based on great compassion. Regarding "thorough reflection":
although the merits of the vows and practices taught in this sutra appear to be shallow discourse concerning conventional truth, in their essential meaning...
Every single point of this ultimate aim originates from the profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas.

If one engages in worldly affairs with the mind of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then every single thing will be none other than the true mark; if one listens to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma with the perfectly wondrous mind, then every single teaching will be none other than the perfectly wondrous.
Should one fail to contemplate this skillfully, there is a fear that one will fall into a shallow understanding of the profound scriptures.
Therefore, one should admonish them. △ Second, receiving the instruction. Mañjuśrī said: "So be it;
we pray that you will speak, for we long to hear it.

△ Third, the section on the actual exposition, divided into two parts: first, answering regarding the name of the Medicine Master Vaidūryaprabha Buddha; second, answering regarding the power of his original vows.
First, regarding the gateway of the virtues:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, "To the east of here, passing through as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Vaidūryanirmala;
the Buddha there is named Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabhā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇa..."
The Perfectly Enlightened One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
In the *Saptabuddha-sūtra*, among the seven Buddhas, counting from the fourth Gaṅgā [Buddha] up to the seventh venerable one, it is [the Buddha of the seventh Gaṅgā].
It flows from beyond ten *gaṅgā*-sands of buddha-fields; this river is named "Heavenly Descent" (*devāvatāra*) for two reasons:

first, because a goddess descended to preside over this river, its name was established through divine manifestation—this is the "Chapter on the Heavenly River" (*Devanadī-parivarta*) found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
second, because the waters of this river branch off from Lake Anavatapta.
Furthermore, as for the source from which it flows downward, its origin is so high that the people cannot fathom it; therefore, this water is named "Coming from Paradise" (Tiāntánglái).
It is just like the waters of our own land, which all originate from the Snow Mountains and reach Mount Jishí.

There, the mountain is so steep and lofty that the water enters the earth and travels underground until it surges forth at the mouth of the Yellow River, becoming the source of the waters of the Middle Kingdom. And yet, the world...

Those who, though having abandoned all evil conduct and practiced wholesome dharmas, were destined for the miserable realms, shall— through the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow—
be brought before him and briefly hear his name. Upon the end of their lives there, they shall return to the human realm, attain right view,
and with diligence and well-disciplined intentions, they shall leave the household life for the homeless state and receive and uphold the teachings within the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

They shall not violate the precepts of training; possessing right view and extensive learning, they will understand profound meanings, be free from overweening pride, refrain from slandering the true Dharma, and avoid becoming companions of Māra.
By practicing the various bodhisattva deeds in successive stages, they will swiftly attain full perfection.
This pertains to the monastic community; the corruption of the Dharma path continues until one falls into wrong views and the evil realms before it ceases.

The reason why the Buddha must not abandon them but allows them to briefly hear the Name is that they originally received the precepts and the training in concentration, wisdom, and morality within the Tathāgata’s Dharma. The rest can be understood accordingly. △ Second.
Avarice and envy.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if there are sentient beings who are stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious, praising themselves and disparaging others, they shall fall into the three evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings for immeasurable thousands of years. Having undergone those intense sufferings, they will pass away from that state.

In future lives among humans, they will become oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys, constantly subjected to whipping and prodding, tormented by hunger and thirst, and always forced to carry heavy loads along the roads.
Or, if they obtain human birth, they will dwell in the lowest and most base conditions as servants or slaves, subject to the驱使 (driving and service) of others, never possessing autonomy.
If, in their previous human existence, they had heard of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha...
By virtue of these wholesome causes, I now recall the Name and take refuge with a sincere heart.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, one is liberated from all sufferings; the faculties become sharp and keen, and wisdom and learning increase.

One constantly seeks the supreme Dharma, always encounters virtuous friends, forever severs the snares of Māra, breaks the shell of ignorance, dries up the river of afflictions, and is liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and grief.
Suffering and affliction arise from the mark of envy. Envy originates in stinginess and greed; because of the craving for profit and status, it manifests through the mouth in four ways:
first, praising oneself and disparaging others, such as when the high official Grand Master Cai slandered Qu Yuan. Indeed, the greedy person’s seizing of others’ wealth is fundamentally...

When one must repay past debts with the physical strength, flesh, and blood of one's own body, and is constantly deprived of autonomy while subjected to the lashes of others, it was because one formerly forcibly seized the property of others, either by threatening them with knives and clubs or by causing them distress through slander.
Therefore, one must now repay that [debt] by undergoing this lack of autonomy and being subjected to the lashes. △ Three.
Hateful and malicious.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if there are sentient beings who delight in causing estrangement and engage in mutual strife and litigation, thereby harassing themselves and others;
who, through body, speech, and mind, create and increase various kinds of evil karma, constantly acting to the detriment of one another—

Seeking further advantage, they conspire with one another to harm each other; they summon deities dwelling in mountains, forests, trees, and burial mounds to kill various sentient beings and take their flesh and blood to offer as sacrifice to yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas.

They write down the names of their enemies and fashion images of them, then curse them with malevolent incantations, using sorcery and the practice of *gū-dhā* (poisonous charms) to commandeer walking corpses (*vetāla*) to cut off the enemy's life and bring about their ruin.
If those sentient beings whose bodies [are afflicted] should hear the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha,
none of those evil matters shall be able to harm them; all will instead give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness toward one another, seeking their benefit and peace,
free from any intent to harm or resentment, each rejoicing and finding contentment in what they themselves receive.
They encroach upon one another while simultaneously seeking mutual benefit.
To delight in discord and rejoice in separation is the internal manifestation of the mind of hatred (*dveṣa*).

While all people of the world prefer harmony and rejoice in union, this person, driven by the mind of hatred, takes particular pleasure in being at odds with others and in distancing himself from them; from time to time, he desires to harm everyone.
To harbor resentment and enmity toward one another, engaging in mutual strife and litigation, is the external manifestation of hatred (*dveṣa*). This is divided into two parts:

first, strife and litigation arising from the Yang; second, toxic harm arising from the Yin. When the Yang force is insufficient while the mind of hatred intensifies further, it inevitably leads to making accusations and incantations to raise the dead.
Furthermore, the terms "mutual" and "one another" are used to indicate that this applies reciprocally.

It is as if the entire world were blind and possessed by anger, such that not a single person with wisdom exists who, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, would refrain from harming those previously harmed.
This refers to the fact that they do not suffer the harm [they intended].

However, as stated in the Universal Gate Chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), it is even more excellent than that to now give rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward all and mutually benefit one another.
With the ear, one rightly governs the obstacle of anger through a mind of loving-kindness; being free from resentment, one does not take pleasure in discord.
It goes without saying that those who commit offenses and reach this state will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms, as their retribution for illness is not explicitly mentioned here.

Having thus completed the explanation of the efficacy of the medicine in uprooting the evil diseases of the three poisons. △ Second, the arising of two virtuous qualities, divided into two parts: first, assisting...
The arising of pure goodness is further twofold:

first, responding to the needs of sentient beings. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if there are members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as other sons and daughters of good family with pure faith who are able to receive and uphold the eightfold [precepts]...
Those who observe the fast and precepts for either one year or three months, upholding and training in the rules of discipline, and who, by these roots of goodness,
vow to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha to hear the True Dharma, yet have not yet reached certainty—
The two characters "unfixed" (*wei-ding*) are precisely the karmic trigger for invoking the power of Bhaisajyaguru. II. Showing the Response, in Two Parts:
A. Birth in the Pure Land:
If one hears the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, at the time of death, there will be eight great...
There were eight great bodhisattvas by name— Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, Ratnakusuma Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,

They are spontaneously born amidst various multicolored flowers made of many jewels.
Those who assist in rebirth— whether as the presiding host of a Pure Land, as an auxiliary in the Western Paradise,
as a fellow-vow holder of Bhaisajyaguru, or as a crown prince in this Sahā world— all share a single power of aspiration to guide and lead future generations.
The worthy one may know this. △ Second, the proximate arising of the ten wholesome actions:

Some, because of this, are born in the heavens; yet even though they are born in the heavens, their original roots of goodness are not yet exhausted, and they do not again take birth in other evil realms.
When their lifespan in the heavens ends, they return to be born among humans, perhaps as a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
Sovereign in majesty and power over the four continents, he establishes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action;
or else they are born into great families of kṣatriyas, brahmins, or householders, possessing abundant wealth and overflowing storehouses,
with handsome features, a full retinue, and being intelligent, wise, courageous, and powerful like mighty warriors.
The character "jiā" (家) should not be read as the character "gū" (姑). △ Second, regarding women transforming their female bodies into male ones:
if a woman hears the name of the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha Tathāgata, and receives and maintains it with a sincere heart, she shall never again receive a female body hereafter.
A Bodhisattva must practice until the completion of an *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa before they can finally eliminate the obstacle of the female body;
yet now, upon hearing the Buddha’s name, one immediately becomes free from it—how great is the power of this merit!

Furthermore, although the cultivation of wholesome states is here discussed solely in terms of karmic retribution, it necessarily requires the internal causes and conditions of wholesome karma to fully realize the fruit. This general outline intends to universally uproot the three obstacles.

The above detailed exposition of the merits of the Original Vow is like a decoction that thoroughly treats the illnesses of the three obstructions of sentient beings and gives rise to the virtues of the two kinds of goodness. △ Third, revealing the merits by means of the *nenbutsu*: The merits of the *nenbutsu* are like a medicinal powder. Just as a medicinal powder is easy to ingest and quickly produces its effect, so too the merit of the *nenbutsu* is easily received and swiftly brings about the benefit of birth in the Pure Land. This is because it is the most excellent practice for those of dull faculties and heavy karmic obstacles. It is said: "The *nenbutsu* is the supreme medicine; it is the king of all practices. Furthermore, the merits of the *nenbutsu* are like a precious jewel. Just as a precious jewel possesses immeasurable value and can eliminate all poverty and suffering, so too the merit of the *nenbutsu* is immeasurable and can eradicate all afflictions and karmic hindrances. It is said: "The *nenbutsu* is the supreme treasure; it is the king of all dharmas. Moreover, the merits of the *nenbutsu* are like a great drum. Just as a great drum’s sound reaches far and wide and awakens all who hear it, so too the merit of the *nenbutsu* pervades the ten directions and awakens all sentient beings. It is said: "The *nenbutsu* is the supreme drum; it is the king of all sounds. Thus, the merits of the *nenbutsu* are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Fourth, revealing the merits by means of the Three Refuges: The merits of the Three Refuges are like a protective armor. Just as wearing armor protects one from all weapons and enemies, so too the merit of the Three Refuges protects one from all evil paths and calamities. It is said: "The Three Refuges are the supreme armor; they are the king of all protections. Furthermore, the merits of the Three Refuges are like a bridge. Just as a bridge connects this shore to the other shore and allows one to cross over all difficulties, so too the merit of the Three Refuges connects the shore of birth and death to the shore of Nirvana and allows one to cross over all suffering. It is said: "The Three Refuges are the supreme bridge; they are the king of all crossings. Moreover, the merits of the Three Refuges are like a boat. Just as a boat carries people across the great ocean and reaches the land of safety, so too the merit of the Three Refuges carries sentient beings across the sea of birth and death and reaches the land of the Buddha. It is said: "The Three Refuges are the supreme boat; they are the king of all conveyances. Thus, the merits of the Three Refuges are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Fifth, revealing the merits by means of the Five Precepts: The merits of the Five Precepts are like a foundation. Just as a foundation supports a building and prevents it from collapsing, so too the merit of the Five Precepts supports the mind and prevents it from falling into the evil paths. It is said: "The Five Precepts are the supreme foundation; they are the king of all virtues. Furthermore, the merits of the Five Precepts are like a lamp. Just as a lamp dispels darkness and illuminates the way, so too the merit of the Five Precepts dispels the darkness of ignorance and illuminates the path to liberation. It is said: "The Five Precepts are the supreme lamp; they are the king of all lights. Moreover, the merits of the Five Precepts are like a mirror. Just as a mirror reflects images clearly and without distortion, so too the merit of the Five Precepts reflects the true nature of reality without error. It is said: "The Five Precepts are the supreme mirror; they are the king of all reflections. Thus, the merits of the Five Precepts are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Sixth, revealing the merits by means of the Ten Good Deeds: The merits of the Ten Good Deeds are like a field. Just as a fertile field yields abundant harvests and provides sustenance for all, so too the merit of the Ten Good Deeds yields the fruit of Buddhahood and provides nourishment for all sentient beings. It is said: "The Ten Good Deeds are the supreme field; they are the king of all blessings. Furthermore, the merits of the Ten Good Deeds are like a river. Just as a great river flows continuously and never ceases, so too the merit of the Ten Good Deeds flows on eternally without interruption. It is said: "The Ten Good Deeds are the supreme river; they are the king of all streams. Moreover, the merits of the Ten Good Deeds are like a tree. Just as a great tree provides shade and fruit for all who pass beneath it, so too the merit of the Ten Good Deeds provides the shade of peace and the fruit of liberation for all sentient beings. It is said: "The Ten Good Deeds are the supreme tree; they are the king of all growth. Thus, the merits of the Ten Good Deeds are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Seventh, revealing the merits by means of the Six Paramitas: The merits of the Six Paramitas are like a chariot. Just as a chariot is drawn by strong horses and travels swiftly to its destination, so too the merit of the Six Paramitas is driven by the power of wisdom and swiftly reaches the city of Nirvana. It is said: "The Six Paramitas are the supreme chariot; they are the king of all vehicles. Furthermore, the merits of the Six Paramitas are like a sun. Just as the sun shines universally upon all things and dispels the cold of winter, so too the merit of the Six Paramitas shines upon all sentient beings and dispels the cold of ignorance. It is said: "The Six Paramitas are the supreme sun; they are the king of all luminaries. Moreover, the merits of the Six Paramitas are like a wind. Just as a great wind blows freely and unimpededly throughout the world, so too the merit of the Six Paramitas circulates freely and unimpededly throughout the realms of existence. It is said: "The Six Paramitas are the supreme wind; they are the king of all movements. Thus, the merits of the Six Paramitas are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Eighth, revealing the merits by means of the Four Immeasurables: The merits of the Four Immeasurables are like a cloud. Just as a great cloud gathers rain and benefits all crops, so too the merit of the Four Immeasurables gathers the rain of Dharma and benefits all sentient beings. It is said: "The Four Immeasurables are the supreme cloud; they are the king of all coverings. Furthermore, the merits of the Four Immeasurables are like a spring. Just as a spring flows with pure water and quenches all thirst, so too the merit of the Four Immeasurables flows with the water of compassion and quenches the thirst of affliction. It is said: "The Four Immeasurables are the supreme spring; they are the king of all moisture. Moreover, the merits of the Four Immeasurables are like a moon. Just as the moon is cool and bright and delights all who behold it, so too the merit of the Four Immeasurables is cool and bright and delights all sentient beings. It is said: "The Four Immeasurables are the supreme moon; they are the king of all joys. Thus, the merits of the Four Immeasurables are inconceivable and beyond measure. One should know this. △ Ninth, revealing the merits by means of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment: The merits of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are like a ladder. Just as a ladder allows one to ascend to a high place and see the distant view, so too the merit of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment allows one to ascend to the stage of Bodhisattvahood and perceive the profound Dharma. It is said: "The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are the supreme ladder; they are the king of all ascents. Furthermore, the merits of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are like a net. Just as a net catches fish and prevents them from escaping, so too the merit of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment catches sentient beings and prevents them from falling back into the cycle of birth and death. It is said: "The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are the supreme net; they are the king of all catchers. Moreover, the merits of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are like a bellows. Just as a bellows fans the fire and causes it to blaze forth, so too the merit of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment fans the fire of wisdom and causes it to burn brightly. It is said: "The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are the supreme bellows; they are the king of all inflammers. Within a single mote of dust, all medicinal powers are fully present. One who can take it attains merit equal to that of the manifest [teachings]; therefore, there exists the "Secret Wheel" deity.
The mantra-explanation in the Tang translation originally lacked these four hundred-odd characters from here until "do not let them be neglected or forgotten.
Later generations supplemented this with text taken from the *Saptabuddhaka-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Seven Buddhas), so as to manifest that the two wheels of this scripture operate in tandem;
when combined, they are doubly excellent. This is divided into three parts: first, indicating the intent; second, the formal exposition; and third, the concluding exhortation. Now...
First. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha attained awakening, by the power of his original vow,
he beheld all sentient beings encountering various sufferings of illness— such as emaciation, wasting away, and jaundice— or being afflicted by...
For those afflicted by demonic possession, enchantments, or *gū* poisons, who may suffer premature death or untimely demise, if one desires to eliminate such suffering and fulfill their aspirations,
[the practice of] *kṣaya* (drying up) is as follows:
the symptoms of the disease of thirst are such that, as described in the *Yogācāra*, a single drop of cool water can [quench it].

"Removing hunger and thirst and eliminating [illness] is this; curing disease is the merit; the fulfillment of what one seeks and desires is the single phrase that immediately gives rise to wholesome virtue.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called "Eliminating the Suffering and Affliction of All Sentient Beings";
having entered this meditative concentration, a great radiance issued forth from within his uṣṇīṣa.

*Namaḥ bhagavate vīrasena vaiḍūryaprabhā-rājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksambuddhāya*. Three times.
Regarding the *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is as follows: *Tadyathā oṃ viśve viśve viśva-samantādgate svāhā*. Each secret mantra has its own specific purpose;
the Great Master Tiantai has already explained this in terms of the four *siddhāntas*, so there is no need to cite them here at length.

It has already been explained that the merits of the original vows are non-dual and without distinction; however, because they are discussed from the perspective of the esoteric, their profound secrecy is further revealed.
Thus, while they are expressed through explicit terminology, they are again presented in a secret manner. Now, let us first analyze the words of the text.
The preceding portion consists of verses of homage, which also pertain to liberation. From "tadyathā" onwards is the esoteric language (*mantra*). "Namo" is translated as... [text ends]
Taking refuge in Bhagavat constitutes the beginning of the general introduction. The first three characters, *Bhagavān*, contain six meanings; therefore, they are not translated [into Chinese].
Some call it *Pójiāfàn* (婆伽梵), while others call it *Pójiāfá* (婆伽伐); these are merely differences between the "Chū" (楚) and "Xià" (夏) dialects of the Sanskrit pronunciation.

The previous version used only three characters, whereas the current version adds one character, *Dì* (帝), which is a drawn-out nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the Sanskrit sound *ṣa*. [This is according to] the Esoteric Section.
In some versions, it is called *vaidūrya* or *sphāṭika*, both of which carry this same meaning.
Because the Dharma Master Xuanzang traveled extensively through the Five Indic Regions and mastered the Sanskrit sounds, his new translations into Chinese use slightly different phonetic characters.
*Vaiḍūrya* refers to the medicinal lapis lazuli; it is also called *vaiḍūrya*, translated as "emperor" (*di*).
